items.name: Three key benefits
items.body: Five benefit claims lead the page: simple, lightweight, privacy, open source, EU-hosted.
items.why: Three claims establish a pattern a reader can act on. A fourth reads as protesting too much and invites scepticism.
items.citation: Shu, S. B., & Carlson, K. A. When three charms but four alarms: Identifying the optimal number of claims in persuasion settings. Journal of Marketing (January 2014).

items.name: Strong but imperfect rating
items.body: No rating shown; star glyph count is 0, so no average to judge.
items.why: A perfect score reads as curated. A few imperfections are what make the rest credible.
items.stat: Sales peak at 4–4.5 stars, then decline.
items.citation: Maslowska, E., Malthouse, E. C., & Bernritter, S. F. Too good to be true: the role of online reviews’ features in probability to buy. International Journal of Advertising (June 2016).

items.name: A decoy plan
items.body: Growth at $14 adds real features; no middle plan is clearly dominated.
items.why: A dominated option makes the target plan the obvious choice without changing its price.
items.stat: Adding a decoy plan boosted main-plan sales by 16–23%.
items.citation: Cui, Y. G., Kim, S. S., & Kim, J. Impact of preciseness of price presentation on the magnitude of compromise and decoy effects. Journal of Business Research (August 2021).
